name: State Machines

hero.title: The spinner and the error, on screen together? Not any more.
hero.lede: A machine is a signal that can only hold the states you declare and only moves along the events you allow. Read it like any signal, render from `matches()`, and let `can()` and `nextEvents()` enable the buttons. Against XState it sends events 34.7× faster.

facts.value: a signal with declared states<small>`machine()` reads it; effects and JSX track it.</small>
34.7× faster `send`<small>bun, one run; faster on all four ops.</small>
states and events inferred<small>No codegen, no typegen file.</small>
{dot:warn}iOS and Android, experimental<small>Compiles to a native `PyreonMachine`.</small>

items.title: One value, not four flags
items.text: `loading`, `error` and `done` can all be true when a slow response lands after a retry. A machine is in exactly one state, and an event the current state doesn't handle changes nothing.

items.title: Buttons that know when they work
items.text: `can('PAY', payload)` runs the guard and predicts exactly what `send` would do; `nextEvents()` lists what is possible now. Both are reactive, so `disabled={() => !checkout.can('PAY')}` stays right.

items.title: Branch states, no glue
items.text: `always: [{ target: 'empty', guard: () => cart().length === 0 }, 'ready']` routes the moment a state is entered, reading ordinary signals. `send` returns the settled state after the cascade.

items.title: No actor to start
items.text: No interpreter, no `createActor().start()`, no context object. Data lives in signals beside the machine; side effects hang off `onEnter`, `onExit` and `onTransition`.

before.label: boolean flags
before.caption: Nothing stops two of these being true. This snippet runs and prints both.

after.label: with @pyreon/machine
after.caption: Only the transitions you wrote can happen. `FETCH` while loading does nothing.
after.code:
import { createMachine } from '@pyreon/machine'
import { effect } from '@pyreon/reactivity'

const fetcher = createMachine({
  initial: 'idle',
  states: {
    idle: { on: { FETCH: 'loading' } },
    loading: { on: { SUCCESS: 'done', ERROR: 'error' } },
    error: { on: { RETRY: 'loading' } },
    done: { final: true },
  },
})

effect(() => console.log(fetcher())) // it is a signal; no actor to start

fetcher.send('FETCH') // 'loading'
fetcher.send('FETCH') // not handled in 'loading': stays 'loading'
console.log(fetcher.matches('loading'), fetcher.can('SUCCESS'))

items.name: `createMachine({ initial, states })`
items.text: with state and event names inferred from the config.

items.name: `send(event, payload?)`
items.text: returns the settled state; unhandled events are no-ops.

items.name: Guards
items.text: `{ target, guard }`; a guard that throws denies instead of crashing `send`.

items.name: Eventless `always` transitions
items.text: for branch states; a runaway loop throws after 1,000 steps.

items.name: Lifecycle listeners
items.text: `onEnter`, `onExit` (before the next `onEnter`), `onTransition`; each returns an unsubscribe.

items.name: Run to completion
items.text: an event sent from inside a listener is queued and handled after the current one, in order.

items.name: `StateOf` / `EventOf`
items.text: type helpers that work on an instance or a config.

limits.title: Data lives in signals
limits.text: There is no `context`. Keep fetched data and errors in signals beside the machine and update them in `onEnter`.

limits.title: Flat by design
limits.text: No hierarchical or parallel states, invoked actors or delayed `after` transitions. Compose several machines with effects when you need them, or use XState for statecharts.

limits.title: `dispose()` clears listeners
limits.text: It removes `onEnter`, `onExit`, `onTransition` and `onDone` callbacks; the machine itself still answers `send`.

benchmarks.rival: vs XState 5.33 · bun / JavaScriptCore, one process per op
benchmarks.h: 34.7× faster `send` than XState, and faster on all four ops.
benchmarks.p: A machine here is a constrained signal, not an interpreter with an actor model, so it does less work per event. It also does less: no statecharts, no actors. Compare features before you compare numbers.

comingFrom.title: Same states block. No actor, no event objects.
comingFrom.after:
import { createMachine } from '@pyreon/machine'
import { effect } from '@pyreon/reactivity'

const fetcher = createMachine({
  initial: 'idle',
  states: {
    idle: { on: { FETCH: 'loading' } },
    loading: { on: { SUCCESS: 'done', ERROR: 'error' } },
    error: { on: { RETRY: 'loading' } },
    done: { final: true },
  },
})

effect(() => console.log(fetcher())) // it is a signal; no actor to start

fetcher.send('FETCH') // 'loading'
fetcher.send('FETCH') // not handled in 'loading': stays 'loading'
console.log(fetcher.matches('loading'), fetcher.can('SUCCESS'))
comingFrom.note: The `states` config ports almost line for line (`type: 'final'` becomes `final: true`). `send({ type })` becomes `send(type, payload?)`, and the machine is read like a signal. Statecharts, context and actors have no equivalent here; if you use them, keep XState.

recipes.title: A checkout that routes itself
recipes.text: A branch state reads the cart and the user, a guard checks the payment payload, and `onTransition` logs every hop.

faq.q: Why is it so much faster than XState?
faq.a: It does less: no actor system, no snapshot objects, no statechart semantics. A transition is a lookup and a signal write. The figures are one overnight run under bun that we wrote; run `packages/fundamentals/machine/bench/` yourself.

faq.q: Does it work in effects and JSX?
faq.a: Yes. `machine()`, `matches()`, `can()`, `nextEvents()` and `isFinal()` are reactive reads, like any signal.

faq.q: Can I send an event from a listener?
faq.a: Yes. It is queued and handled after the current transition finishes, in order; more than 10,000 in one `send` throws a runaway error.
